headings.title: Introduction and Classification of Abortion
headings.content: Abortion, defined as the termination of pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation or the expulsion of a fetus weighing less than 500 grams, remains a critical public health issue in Nigeria. Clinical classifications categorize abortion broadly into spontaneous and induced types. Spontaneous abortion, commonly known as miscarriage, occurs naturally due to chromosomal anomalies, maternal systemic illnesses, or anatomical abnormalities. Induced abortions are intentional terminations, which can be further subdivided into safe, legal procedures performed by trained healthcare professionals in sanitary environments, and unsafe, clandestine procedures performed by unqualified individuals or under unsanitary conditions. Unsafe abortions are particularly prevalent in resource-limited settings due to restrictive legal frameworks, societal stigma, and limited access to contraceptive services. Understanding this classification is vital for nursing students, as the etiology and legal context directly dictate the clinical presentation and the likelihood of severe complications. Nurses must approach patients with a non-judgmental, empathetic attitude, recognizing that timely identification of the abortion type guides subsequent clinical interventions. Furthermore, recognizing the statistical burden of unsafe abortion in West Africa helps student nurses appreciate the importance of preventive health education, robust family planning counseling, and the provision of compassionate, evidence-based post-abortion care in Nigerian hospitals and primary healthcare centers.

headings.title: Immediate Complications: Hemorrhage and Shock
headings.content: Hemorrhage and shock represent the most acute and life-threatening immediate complications following an abortion. Excessive bleeding can arise from incomplete evacuation of products of conception, uterine atony, coagulopathies, or direct vascular trauma during surgical interventions. In Nigerian clinical practice, delayed presentation of incomplete or unsafe abortions frequently culminates in severe hypovolemic shock if prompt medical and surgical resuscitation is not initiated. Nursing students must be highly vigilant in monitoring vital signs, keeping a close eye on parameters such as falling blood pressure, tachycardia, tachypnea, and altered mental status. Blood loss estimation is notoriously inaccurate; therefore, nurses must assess systemic perfusion signs, including cool, clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, and oliguria. Immediate management requires establishing large-bore intravenous access, drawing blood for hemoglobin, hematocrit, and cross-matching, and initiating aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids alongside oxytocic medications to stimulate uterine contraction. Blood transfusions may be urgently required. Furthermore, emergency surgical evacuation of retained products of conception is often necessary to stop the source of bleeding. Understanding the physiological cascades of hypovolemic shock enables nurses to anticipate complications and collaborate effectively with multidisciplinary medical teams to save maternal lives.

headings.title: Infectious Complications: Sepsis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
headings.content: Infectious complications are exceptionally common, particularly following unsafe clandestine abortions performed with unsterilized instruments or non-sterile substances introduced into the uterine cavity. Microorganisms ascend from the lower genital tract, leading to endometritis, parametritis, pelvic peritonitis, and generalized sepsis. Patients typically present with lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, purulent lochia, fever, chills, and uterine tenderness upon palpation. If left untreated, localized infections can progress rapidly to septic shock, multi-organ dysfunction syndrome, and death. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) can also develop as a sequela, leading to chronic pelvic pain, tubal factor infertility, and an increased risk of future ectopic pregnancies. Nursing care centers on obtaining high-vaginal and endocervical swabs for culture and sensitivity before initiating broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy as prescribed. Nurses must meticulously monitor vital signs for spikes in temperature or signs of hemodynamic instability, record accurate fluid intake and output, and manage pain effectively. Strict adherence to aseptic technique during all nursing procedures is mandatory to prevent cross-contamination. Educating the patient on completing the full course of antibiotics and maintaining proper perineal hygiene is vital for full recovery and long-term reproductive health preservation.

headings.title: Traumatic Complications: Uterine Perforation and Organ Damage
headings.content: Traumatic complications occur predominantly during surgical evacuation procedures, particularly when performed by unskilled providers or during advanced gestations in uncoordinated settings. Uterine perforation is the most frequent structural injury, where surgical instruments such as uterine sounds, dilators, or suction curettes breach the myometrial wall. Perforations can be categorized as minor, requiring only conservative observation and antibiotic coverage, or major, which involve injury to adjacent abdominal and pelvic organs such as the bowel, bladder, broad ligament, or major pelvic blood vessels. Risk factors include a retroverted or anteverted uterus, cervical stenosis, prior uterine scarring, and operator inexperience. Clinical signs of uterine perforation include sudden, severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the procedure, unexpected ease of instrument insertion beyond expected depth, free intraperitoneal fluid, or the visualization of extra-uterine tissue (such as bowel or omentum) retrieved from the uterine cavity. Nurses must be alert to post-operative complaints of worsening abdominal pain, abdominal guarding, rebound tenderness, or signs of acute abdomen. Management often ranges from conservative observation with close serial abdominal examinations to emergency exploratory laparotomy for organ repair and hemostasis.

headings.title: Delayed and Long-Term Complications
headings.content: Beyond immediate acute crises, complications of abortion can manifest weeks, months, or even years later, severely impacting a woman's long-term health and psychosocial well-being. Anatomical sequelae include Asherman's syndrome, characterized by the formation of intrauterine adhesions resulting from aggressive curettage or infection, which can cause secondary amenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, recurrent pregnancy loss, and infertility. Cervical incompetence, resulting from forced mechanical cervical dilation during surgical evacuation, predisposes women to second-trimester miscarriages and preterm births in subsequent pregnancies. Chronic pelvic pain resulting from unresolved low-grade pelvic inflammatory disease is another debilitating physical consequence. In addition to physical complications, psychological and emotional sequelae are profound. Women may experience post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, complicated grief, and depression, particularly in environments marked by heavy social stigma, lack of support, or judgmental healthcare attitudes. Nurses play a crucial role in holistic care by conducting thorough history-taking during follow-up visits, screening for psychological distress, providing empathetic counseling, and making appropriate referrals to mental health professionals or specialized fertility clinics.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Clinical Evaluation
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment and clinical evaluation form the cornerstone of safe, effective care for patients presenting with suspected or confirmed abortion complications. The nurse begins with a focused health history, establishing the exact gestational age, the onset and nature of symptoms such as bleeding and pain, and whether the abortion was spontaneous or induced. A detailed obstetric and gynecological history helps identify pre-existing risk factors. Physical examination includes a systematic primary survey (ABCDE approach) to evaluate hemodynamic stability, followed by vital sign recording and an abdominal examination to check for tenderness, guarding, or distension. A sterile speculum examination and bimanual exam are performed by skilled clinicians to assess the state of the cervix, estimate uterine size, and identify retained products of conception or active bleeding; nurses assist by preparing equipment, ensuring patient comfort, and providing emotional support. Diagnostic investigations ordered include a complete blood count (CBC) to check for anemia or infection, blood grouping and cross-matching for potential transfusion, serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels, and a pelvic ultrasound to visualize the uterine cavity. Throughout the evaluation, nurses must maintain strict confidentiality, practice active listening, and provide clear explanations of each procedure to alleviate patient anxiety.

headings.title: Emergency Management and Post-Abortion Care
headings.content: Emergency management and post-abortion care (PAC) are essential components of comprehensive nursing practice aimed at reducing maternal morbidity and mortality. Emergency protocols dictate immediate stabilization of unstable patients through fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion, broad-spectrum antibiotics for infection control, and surgical intervention (such as manual vacuum aspiration or dilation and curettage) to evacuate retained products of conception. Once the acute crisis is managed, holistic post-abortion care takes precedence. PAC encompasses compassionate counseling, addressing emotional needs, and offering contraceptive services before discharge to prevent repeat unintended pregnancies. Nurses play a pivotal role in providing contraceptive counseling tailored to the patient's lifestyle and reproductive goals, ranging from barrier methods to long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs). Pain management protocols using prescribed analgesics must be implemented to ensure physical comfort. Furthermore, nurses provide essential discharge instructions detailing warning signs that require immediate medical attention—such as heavy vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge, or fever—and schedule a follow-up appointment to evaluate physical recovery and psychological well-being, reinforcing a supportive continuum of care.
